summary: A draft Military Supplement to the ISO Transport Protocol (IS 8072 and IS 8073), giving conventions, option choices and parameter values. It was circulated to gather comments, with the note that it might not matter directly to Internet research but could interest implementors.

plainLanguage.summary: The ISO transport rulebook has many options. This memo picks the settings the military wanted to use, so everyone's equipment works together.

subtitle: Configuration guide for ISO Transport Protocol Classes 2 and 4 in DOD networks.

tldr.problem: The ISO Transport Protocol (IS 8072 and IS 8073) defines five classes of service with many options and configuration choices, but does not mandate specific settings, leaving implementors to guess what works for military interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This supplement specifies the transport classes (2 and 4), mandatory and optional procedures, parameter values, and configuration conventions that military DOD implementations should follow when operating over both connection-oriented and connectionless network services.
tldr.outcome: Military systems implementing these conventions can ensure equipment interchangeability and enable host-to-host connectivity across network boundaries while maintaining survivability in communication.

facts.label: Transport classes
facts.value: Class 0 through Class 4; supplement covers Classes 2 and 4

today: RFC 1007 is an informational RFC from June 1987 that circulated a draft military supplement to the ISO Transport Protocol for comment. It does not establish an Internet standard but documents conventions important to DOD implementors.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The ISO Transport Protocol, defined in standards IS 8072 (service definition) and IS 8073 (protocol specification), provides a message transport layer that sits above IP and other network services. It supports five classes of service (0 through 4), each with different capabilities and error recovery mechanisms.

This supplement specifies conventions, option selections, and parameter values for implementations operating within DOD (Department of Defense) packet-switched data networks, including Local Area Networks (LANs). It mandates the use of Transport Protocol Classes 4 and 2 and the connectionless network service (IS 8473) across network and subnetwork boundaries. The supplement covers both connection-oriented network services (CONS) and connectionless network services (CLNS, such as IP).

The document provides formal definitions in five sections: scope and purpose, referenced standards, definitions and acronyms, general requirements and option selections, and special addressing and reference number conventions. It does not provide full implementation detail, instead referring to a separate Implementation Guide for guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISO transport standard lets vendors choose many settings. This memo says which settings the military requires so everyone's equipment works together across the network.

sections.title: Classes of Service and Mandatory Procedures
sections.content:
The ISO Transport Protocol defines five classes: Class 0 (basic), Class 1 (error recovery over unreliable networks), Class 2 (multiplexing over reliable networks), Class 3 (error recovery with multiplexing), and Class 4 (error recovery and multiplexing over unreliable networks). This supplement applies only to Classes 2 and 4.

Class 2 requires a connection-oriented network service and provides flow control, multiplexing, and expedited data transfer. Class 4 can operate over either connection-oriented or connectionless network services and adds error recovery with checksums and retransmission.

The supplement mandates conformance requirements: a system must implement Class 2 or Class 0 (or both) if operating over CONS, or Class 4 if operating over CLNS. If a system implements Class 4 over CONS, it must also implement Class 2. Implementations must handle all Connect Request (CR) and Connect Confirm (CC) protocol data units (TPDUs) correctly, support all mandatory procedures, and optionally support additional procedures for which they claim conformance.
sections.plainLanguage: Class 2 is for reliable networks and does many things. Class 4 is for unreliable networks and recovers from errors. Military networks must support Class 2 for wired connections and Class 4 for any network, including unreliable ones.

sections.title: Negotiated Options and Parameter Selection
sections.content:
Eight negotiated options are determined during connection setup between peer transport entities. Class of service: Implementations shall offer Class 2 if using CONS and must reject proposals for Class 1 or 3. Extended formats: Implementations shall always propose and accept extended formats for sequence numbering (range 0 to 2^31 - 1) and flow control credit (0 to 2^16 - 1) instead of normal formats. Expedited data: Support is mandatory in Class 2. Maximum TPDU size: Must be chosen from a defined list (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, or 8192 octets) and all smaller values must also be supported. Checksum use: Mandatory for Class 4; optional for Class 2. Checksums should be used with IP on concatenated networks and always when encryption is used, but not required for high performance unless error rates demand it. Protection parameters: Not defined in this supplement. Flow control in Class 2: Shall always be proposed and accepted. Service quality parameters: Not defined except for residual error rate and priority (which are under consideration).

For Class 4 over connectionless networks, implementations must support flow control credit withdrawal, flow control confirmation, and subsequenced acknowledgements to manage resources among connections of varying priority. Class 4 over CONS may use multiple network connections (splitting) for better performance and resilience.
sections.plainLanguage: When two systems connect, they negotiate what features to use: which class, whether to use error checking, how big messages can be, whether to do flow control. The military rules say what each system must propose and accept.

sections.title: Local Options and Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
Local options are implementation choices visible only to the local system. For Class 2, implementations may elect to multiplex multiple transport connections on a single network connection (but Class 2 and Class 4 should not be multiplexed together). A lockup prevention timer is strongly recommended to prevent deadlock when waiting for a connect confirmation. Protocol errors in Class 2 should cause the connection to terminate without sending an error TPDU.

For Class 4, flow control credit withdrawal is mandatory to manage resource allocation among connections of different priority levels. Subsequenced acknowledgements shall be supported to handle credit withdrawal correctly. Multiplexing of Class 4 connections on a single network connection is permitted but should not mix with Class 2 connections. Concatenation of multiple TPDUs into a single network service data unit is permitted when operating over CLNS with large capacity service data units.

The supplement recommends using a specific optimized checksum algorithm rather than the one in the ISO annex. When a TPDU with a bad checksum is received over CONS, implementations should send a network-level reset rather than disconnect. Over CLNS, bad TPDUs shall simply be discarded. Protocol errors in Class 4 result in a disconnect request if the TPDU is otherwise valid; unrecognized parameters cause disconnect only if the TPDU is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: Each implementation can make local decisions about multiplexing, timeouts, and error recovery, as long as it meets the mandatory requirements. The military provides guidance on safe choices to prevent deadlocks and resource exhaustion.

sections.title: Addressing and Connection Management
sections.content:
The supplement covers three special requirements. Addressing conventions for Transport Service Access Points (TSAPs) and Network Service Access Points (NSAPs) are under consideration for future definition. Transport connection reference numbers must follow a strict convention: implementations shall not reuse a reference number until all numbers in a defined range have been used. If reference numbers are defined as [1,N], a number R used once cannot be used again until R+1 through N, then 1 through R-1 have all been used. This strict cycling, combined with the ISO minimum freeze time requirement, prevents ambiguity and confusion in recovering from failures. A simple implementation approach is documented in the Implementors Guide Part 9.3.

Operation over connectionless network service: Class 4 is designed to work over CLNS (such as IP), handling packet loss and reordering via checksums, acknowledgements, and retransmission. Class 2 over CLNS is not recommended due to insufficient error recovery. Recovery from peer deactivation (crash): The ISO standard does not define connection re-establishment, but the formal descriptions are flexible enough to permit simple adaptations for crash recovery without protocol changes, as described in the Implementors Guide Part 9.2.
sections.plainLanguage: When connection references are reused, the system strictly rotates through all possible numbers to avoid confusion. The military also cares about recovering when a system crashes and comes back up.
